title: How to make a 40-step data infrastructure demo clickable in 10 steps
summary: Cloud, security and data demos average 43 steps and 10.7% completion in a Storylane study. Start from the output and cut the main flow to 10 steps.
body_markdown:
Ask a sales engineer at a data platform to build an interactive demo and you usually get the product in the order it is used. Connect the warehouse. Pick a source. Map the schema. Set the schedule. Add a transformation. Run it. Watch it land. Somewhere around step 38, a dashboard fills with numbers and the buyer finally sees why anyone pays for this. Most buyers never get there. My argument is simple: data infrastructure demos run long because they show setup, and buyers need the result, so start from the output and add back only the steps they ask about. I call it **output first, setup on request** .


## How long are data infrastructure demos?


Longer than everyone else's, and by a lot. In June 2026 our team published[an analysis of demo lengths across 9 industries](https://www.storylane.io/blog/learnings-from-analyzing-demo-lengths-across-9-industries) : 34 interactive demos and 5,409 demo sessions, limited to marketing demos placed on websites. The average demo had 21 steps and a 26% completion rate (completion meaning an engaged viewer reached the final step).


The three most technical industries in the set, cloud computing, cyber security and data technology, averaged 43 steps and 10.7% completion. The three least technical, product, marketing and sales tools, averaged 11 steps and 41% completion.


Group (internal Storylane data, demo-length study) Average steps Completion rate


Top 10% of demos by completion 9 64.02%


Product, marketing and sales tools 11 41%


All 34 demos 21 26%


Bottom 10% of demos by completion 37 1.39%


Cloud, cyber security and data tools 43 10.7%


Be careful with these numbers. Thirty-four demos is a small sample, the study counted website demos rather than demos sales engineers send after a call, and it shows a correlation between length and completion, not proof that cutting steps causes more people to finish. I still think the pattern is worth acting on, because of where those missing 89% stop.


## Why do data infrastructure demos run long?


The obvious explanation is the one the study itself offers: these products sell to technical buyers, and there is simply more to show. That is true, and it doesn't fully fit. A data product is not more complicated to look at than a CRM. It is more complicated to set up. The extra 30 steps are almost all configuration.


I have a theory for why configuration takes over. In infrastructure, setup is where credibility lives. A sales engineer who skips the connector screen worries the buyer will think the connector is hard, or fake. So the demo follows the product's own sequence, because that sequence feels honest. The order of the product becomes the order of the story.


The trouble is what that does to the value. Data infrastructure pays off at the end of a chain: the fresh table, the caught anomaly, the query that came back in seconds. Follow the chain in order and the payoff lands at step 40. That gives you the core problem in one sentence:


**In a setup-first demo, buyers leave before the step that shows why they should care.**


With 10.7% completion, roughly nine in ten viewers of a 43-step demo never reach the last step. When the last step is the result, they leave having seen only the work.


## What does a buyer actually need to see?


Two things, in this order. First, the outcome: what their data looks like once your product is running. Second, enough of the path to believe that outcome is real for them. The second is a smaller set than sales engineers fear. A technical buyer rarely needs to watch every field get filled in. They need to know three things: where this number came from, what happens when something breaks, and how long setup takes.


That is why I'd build the main flow backwards. Start at the output and walk upstream only as far as the buyer's trust requires. Everything else becomes a branch they can open if they want it.


## How to cut a 40-step workflow to 10


Here is the method. The example is illustrative: a made-up data pipeline product, not a real customer demo.


1. **Write out the full workflow.** All 40 steps, in product order. Don't cut yet. For our pipeline tool that runs from login and warehouse credentials, through source selection, schema mapping, sync schedule, transformations and a test run, to monitoring, alerting and the dashboard.
2. **Mark the moment of value.** Find the one screen where the buyer would say "that's what we need". For the pipeline tool it is the dashboard showing data that synced minutes ago, with a clear record that every row arrived.
3. **Make it step one.** Open on that screen with the data already flowing. One sentence of copy says what the buyer is looking at and why it matters to them.
4. **Walk upstream, three or four steps.** Click a number and trace it back: the transformation that shaped it, the sync that delivered it, the source it came from. This is the provenance chain, and it answers "is this real?" without any configuration screens.
5. **Show one failure handled.** Infrastructure buyers buy reliability. One or two steps showing a schema change caught and flagged does more than ten setup screens.
6. **End on how long it takes.** A final step stating what setup involves and roughly how long it takes for a team like theirs, in plain words. That is the question every technical buyer brings.
7. **Move setup into optional flows.** The connector, schema mapping and scheduling screens become separate flows, each titled with the question it answers: "How do I connect my warehouse?", "How does schema mapping work?". Nothing is hidden. It is simply not in the way.


That gives you a main flow of about ten steps, close to the 8 to 12 the study recommends for website demos and the 9 steps the top tenth of demos averaged. The other 30 steps still exist. The buyer now chooses them.


If you are unsure whether to split into flows at all, our earlier piece on[when to break a demo into multiple flows](https://www.storylane.io/blog/single-vs-multi-flow-demos) covers the thresholds.


## Won't technical buyers think we are hiding the hard part?


This is the strongest objection, and it deserves a real answer. Data engineers and platform teams are rightly suspicious of glossy outputs. Show them a perfect dashboard and they will ask what it took to get there.


My answer is that output first is not output only. The setup flows are one click away, named by the question, and the provenance chain in the main flow shows the data has a source. What changes is who decides how much setup to watch. A buyer who wants to see schema mapping opens that flow. A buyer who is still deciding whether the category matters to them sees the result and leaves knowing why it might.


There is a second benefit for the sales engineer. The flows people open tell you what they are worried about before the call. If the warehouse connector flow gets opened and the alerting flow doesn't, you know where to spend the first ten minutes live.


## Where this fits in a presales motion


The study measured website demos, so I am extending it here on judgement. I think the same structure works better for the demo a sales engineer leaves behind after a call. The person who watched you live may follow 40 steps. The colleagues they forward it to won't, and they are the ones you never met. Our post on[demoing technical software to non-technical buyers](https://www.storylane.io/blog/demo-technical-software-non-technical-buyers) goes deeper on that hand-off.


It also helps with the environment problem infrastructure teams know well. A captured, clickable demo doesn't need a live cluster or a seeded warehouse every time someone wants to look. If your product runs in the customer's own environment, see[how to demo on-prem software without shipping a VM](https://www.storylane.io/blog/demo-on-prem-software-without-vm) . If the buyer genuinely needs to type their own queries, a[sandbox environment](https://www.storylane.io/blog/sandbox-environment-software-developer-friendly-demos) is the right tool, and the output-first main flow is a good way to earn that next step. And if the demo uses real-looking data,[strip sensitive customer data](https://www.storylane.io/blog/remove-sensitive-data-from-software-demo) before it leaves the building.


## Building it in Storylane


I work at Storylane, so weigh this section accordingly. Storylane Demo Suite is built for sales engineers who want to capture the product once and present it many ways: a short main flow for the first look, separate flows for setup questions, and the same demo usable on a live call or sent afterwards. That is the output-first structure above, and it is a natural fit for teams selling data, cloud and security products to technical buyers.


## What to do on Monday


Open your longest demo and find the step where the value appears. If it is past step ten, move it to step one, trace the chain back three or four steps, and turn everything else into flows named by the questions buyers ask. Then watch which flows they open. The order of your product is not the order of your buyer's interest, and the demo should follow the buyer.
